questions.stem: Where is Orbital set?
options: Aboard the International Space Station, orbiting the Earth
On a spacecraft carrying six settlers on their way to Mars
At mission control in Houston during a dangerous launch
On a research base on the Moon after a crash landing
questions.explanation: The whole novel takes place on the International Space Station. The crew never leave it, and the Earth is seen only through its windows.

questions.stem: How much time does Orbital cover?
options: A single day, in which the station circles the Earth sixteen times
A whole nine-month mission, from the launch until the landing
A single week, with one long chapter for each day on board
A full year, in which the crew watch all four seasons below
questions.explanation: The novel covers one 24-hour period. The station orbits the Earth about every 90 minutes, so the crew see sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets in a day.

questions.stem: How are the chapters of Orbital organised?
options: Each is a log entry written by the commander for mission control
Each is dated by the calendar, across the many months of the mission
Each follows an orbit, with headings such as 'Orbit 1, ascending'
Each is narrated in the first person by a different crew member
questions.explanation: The chapters are named for the orbits, or parts of orbits, the station makes during the day. The structure follows the station's circling path rather than a dramatic plot.

questions.stem: Who is on board the station in Orbital?
options: Six crew: three astronauts and three Russian cosmonauts
Four crew: two Americans, a Russian and a Chinese astronaut
Six crew, each from a different one of six nations
Six crew: four astronauts and two Russian cosmonauts
questions.explanation: The six are four astronauts, from the United States, Japan, Britain and Italy, and two Russian cosmonauts. Four are men and two are women.

questions.stem: Chie's mother dies while Chie is in orbit. What does this show about life on the station?
options: Astronauts can be flown home within a day when a family emergency arises
Mission control holds back bad news until the mission is over
The crew's work matters more than the lives they left behind
The crew are cut off from their lives on Earth, even in grief
questions.explanation: Chie cannot go home to be with her family. Her grief has to fit inside the station's routine, which shows how far the crew are from the lives they left.

questions.stem: What weather event do the crew watch develop below them through the day?
options: A hurricane in the Atlantic, heading towards Florida
A dust storm crossing the Sahara towards the south of Europe
A typhoon in the Pacific, heading towards the Philippines
A bushfire spreading across south-eastern Australia
questions.explanation: A typhoon builds over the western Pacific and moves towards the Philippines. The crew photograph it on their passes, watching a disaster grow from far above.

questions.stem: What do the crew and the forecasters notice about the typhoon during the day?
options: It weakens and turns away from land, as the forecasters predicted
It grows more slowly than forecast, giving people time to leave
It can be tracked from the ground but not from the station
It grows faster and stronger than the forecasters expected
questions.explanation: The storm develops more quickly than predicted, and the crew see and photograph it from above. From orbit it looks beautiful, which sets the crew's wonder against what it will mean for people on the ground.

questions.stem: Which other space mission is under way on the same day?
options: A crewed mission heading for the Moon
A rescue mission to bring the whole crew home early
A private flight bringing tourists to the station
A robot probe sent to land on one of Jupiter's moons
questions.explanation: A crewed lunar mission sets out during the novel, and the station crew follow it. It reminds them that they are close to home, circling the Earth while others travel further out.

questions.stem: How does the cosmonaut Anton feel about the Moon mission?
options: He is in charge of it, guiding its crew by radio from the space station
He envies its crew, having long dreamed of going to the Moon himself
He thinks it wastes money that should be spent on the space station
He is relieved not to be on it, because he is afraid of the danger
questions.explanation: Anton has dreamed of reaching the Moon, and watching another crew set off stirs his longing. His envy shows that even people in space can feel left behind.

questions.stem: Which pairing of crew member and nationality is correct?
options: Pietro, Italian
Nell, American
Chie, Russian
Roman, Japanese
questions.explanation: Pietro is Italian, Nell is British, Chie is Japanese, Shaun is American, and Roman and Anton are Russian cosmonauts.

questions.stem: Which two crew members look after the mice used in an experiment on board?
options: Shaun and Pietro
Anton and Roman
Roman and Shaun
Chie and Nell
questions.explanation: Chie and Nell care for the mice, which are studied to see how weightlessness affects living bodies. The experiments link the crew's own bodies to the animals they watch.

questions.stem: What is the American astronaut Shaun studying on board?
options: How the typhoon's winds change speed as it nears the coast
How the Moon mission's rocket uses fuel on its journey out
How plants grow when there is no gravity to guide their roots
How the mice on board lose muscle when they are weightless
questions.explanation: Shaun tends small plants to learn how roots grow without gravity. The mice are Chie and Nell's work, which is the most common mix-up.

questions.stem: Shaun keeps a postcard linked to his wife. Which painting is on it?
options: The Last Supper by Leonardo
Las Meninas by Velázquez
The Starry Night by van Gogh
The Great Wave by Hokusai
questions.explanation: Shaun's postcard shows Velázquez's Las Meninas. The painting matters to the novel because of what it does with point of view.

questions.stem: Why does Las Meninas suit the concerns of Orbital?
options: It shows a family gathered at home, like the crew's homesick memories
It uses swirling colour, like cloud patterns seen from orbit
It plays with who is looking at whom, as the crew look back at Earth
It shows a ship caught in a storm at sea, like the typhoon below
questions.explanation: In Las Meninas the painter shows himself painting, and the royal couple appear only in a mirror, where the viewer stands. Orbital is also about viewpoint: humans looking at their own world from outside it.

questions.stem: James Wood called Orbital 'barely a novel'. Which feature of the book is he pointing to?
options: It is told as one unbroken paragraph, with no chapter breaks
It has almost no conventional plot, focusing on reflection instead
It switches genre halfway, from realism into science fiction
It is mostly made up of real NASA documents and transcripts
questions.explanation: Orbital has little conflict or plot: the crew work, eat, sleep and look at the Earth. Some critics see this as a weakness, while others, including the Booker judges, see the meditative style as its strength.

questions.stem: Which prize did Orbital win in 2024?
options: The Stella Prize
The Booker Prize
The Miles Franklin Award
The Pulitzer Prize for Fiction
questions.explanation: Orbital won the 2024 Booker Prize. It was the first novel set in space to win, and one of the shortest winners.

questions.stem: Samantha Harvey described Orbital as a 'space pastoral'. What does this suggest?
options: It is a satire that mocks the cost and vanity of space travel
It is a quiet, reflective book about beauty, not a space adventure
It is a nostalgic novel about the crew's childhoods in the country
It is a thriller in which the crew fight to survive a disaster
questions.explanation: A pastoral is a calm work that celebrates landscape and nature. Harvey uses the term to show that her book is about wonder and the Earth's beauty, not danger and action.

questions.stem: What did Harvey watch while she was writing Orbital?
options: Footage of typhoons filmed by planes flying into the storms
Old science fiction films about astronauts lost in space
A live video stream of the Earth from the space station
Recordings of the first Moon landing, played each morning
questions.explanation: Harvey watched a live feed from the space station to see what the crew would see. The novel's detailed descriptions of the Earth from orbit come from that close attention.

questions.stem: Harvey finished Orbital in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Why might this matter to a reader?
options: It explains why the crew are quarantined after an outbreak on board
It means the typhoon is meant to stand for the spread of the virus
It was a time when space travel halted, which the novel protests
It was a time of isolation, like the crew's life cut off from Earth
questions.explanation: Many people spent 2020 in lockdown, separated from family. A novel about six people in a sealed space, watching the world from a distance, gains extra meaning in that light. The novel is not about the pandemic itself, so the connection is one of resonance rather than allegory.

questions.stem: Astronauts often describe the 'overview effect' after seeing the Earth from space. How does Orbital reflect it?
options: The crew feel the Earth is too large to be harmed by people
The crew see the Earth as one connected, fragile home
The crew lose interest in the Earth and long for deep space
The crew become prouder of their own nations than before
questions.explanation: The overview effect is the shift in thinking that comes from seeing the whole planet at once. In Orbital the crew keep feeling how connected and fragile the Earth is.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to Orbital?
options: The danger of relying on technology to keep human beings alive
The rivalry between nations racing to be first back to the Moon
The cost of fame for astronauts when they return to Earth
The beauty and fragility of the Earth, and our place in the universe
questions.explanation: From orbit the crew see the whole planet, and they keep returning to how beautiful, small and vulnerable it is. The novel uses their view to ask what human life amounts to.

questions.stem: How does Orbital treat human damage to the planet?
options: The crew conclude the changes are natural cycles, not human-made
The crew see signs such as shrinking ice and forests from orbit
The novel lectures readers directly on climate change policy
The damage cannot be seen from orbit and is reported by radio
questions.explanation: Looking down, the crew see evidence of human impact on glaciers, forests and ice sheets. The novel links this damage to human wants and politics, without turning into a lecture.

questions.stem: What does the crew's life together suggest about people from different nations?
options: They put national loyalties first, mirroring rivalries on Earth
They depend on each other completely to survive in a shared space
They cannot work together, so each nation stays in its own section
They compete to finish their experiments before the others do
questions.explanation: The crew come from countries that are often rivals on Earth, yet on the station each life depends on the others. Reviewers have read this as a picture of mutual dependence.

questions.stem: Who narrates Orbital?
options: A third-person narrator who moves among the six crew members' thoughts
Chie, who tells the whole story in the first person after her mother's death
Mission control, which reports on the crew through radio messages
Anton, who writes about the day years later, back on Earth
questions.explanation: The narrator moves freely between the six crew, and at times draws back to describe the Earth itself. This wide view matches the station's view of the whole planet.

questions.stem: Orbital is mostly told in the present tense. What is the effect?
options: It gives a sense of continuous, unfolding time as the station circles
It shows that the events are being remembered long after the mission
It builds suspense about whether the crew will survive the day
It distances the reader, making the crew seem cold and remote
questions.explanation: The present tense keeps the reader inside the day as it happens, orbit by orbit. It suits a book about attention to the moment rather than about what happens next.

questions.stem: What is the effect of building the novel around sixteen orbits?
options: Its orbits mark sixteen separate days of the crew's mission
Its repeated circuits give a rhythm that mirrors the station's path
Its orbits count down to a disaster that ends the novel very suddenly
Its orbits let the story jump forward a month at a time
questions.explanation: Sunrise and sunset come round again and again, and the chapters follow the same loop. Structure and subject match: the form of the book circles like the station.

questions.stem: Harvey describes the station as a 'great metal albatross'. What does the image suggest?
options: The station is noisy and clumsy, unable to stay in the sky
The station glides endlessly around the globe, like a huge seabird
The station is old and rusting, and will soon fall into the sea
The station is lost, searching for somewhere safe to land
questions.explanation: The albatross is famous for gliding vast distances over the ocean. The metaphor makes the station both mechanical and alive, circling the planet without rest.

questions.stem: The novel describes the Earth as 'a mother waiting for her children to return'. What does this image suggest?
options: The Earth depends on the crew, who watch over it like parents
The Earth is the crew's home, which cares for them and awaits them
The Earth is angry with the crew for leaving and will punish them
The Earth is a dangerous place the crew are glad to have escaped
questions.explanation: Personifying the Earth as a mother stresses that the crew belong to it and depend on it. It also makes human damage to the planet feel like harm done to family. The crew depend on the Earth, not the other way round.

questions.stem: What idea does the line 'We matter greatly and not at all' express?
options: Seen from orbit, human life is precious and tiny
Human achievements matter, but individual lives do not
Humans will matter more once they have settled on other planets
Nothing humans do on Earth can be seen from the space station
questions.explanation: The line holds two opposite ideas together. From space, human life looks tiny against the universe, yet the crew feel how much each life matters.

questions.stem: What is surprising about the line 'The earth, from here, is like heaven'?
options: It suggests the crew feel closer to God the higher they go
It contrasts the peaceful station with the troubled Earth
It is said by mission control to cheer up the homesick crew
It finds heaven by looking down at the Earth, not up at the sky
questions.explanation: People usually look up to imagine heaven. The crew, already in the sky, look down and find the Earth itself heavenly, which suggests our world is the paradise we should value.

questions.stem: The novel speaks of the planet being shaped by the 'force of human want'. What does the phrase suggest?
options: Humans want to leave the Earth and will soon abandon it
Human wants matter less than natural forces in shaping the planet
Humans must give up their desires if the planet is to survive
Human desires have changed the whole Earth, for better and worse
questions.explanation: The phrase points to human desire as a force as strong as nature. It covers both the achievements, like the station itself, and the damage the crew can see below.

questions.stem: Harvey stresses that only a thin skin of metal separates the crew from the void. What does the detail emphasise?
options: How thin the barrier is between the crew and death
How heavy the station is compared with the older spacecraft
How advanced the technology is that protects them
How cramped and crowded the crew's living space is
questions.explanation: Outside the hull is a vacuum that would kill the crew instantly. Stressing how little stands between them and space makes their safety feel fragile, like the planet they watch.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Orbital suggests that seeing the Earth from a distance changes how we value it.' Discuss.
options: Harvey shows that the crew's distant view makes the Earth seem more precious and fragile
Orbital is a novel by Samantha Harvey about six astronauts on the space station
This essay will discuss how the Earth is shown in Orbital by Samantha Harvey
Orbital won the Booker Prize in 2024 and is one of the shortest winners ever
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The crew watch a typhoon from the space station.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Retell what each crew member does while the typhoon is building
Explain how the storm looks beautiful from orbit but means danger below
Add the exact wind speed of the typhoon and the day it formed
List the other things the crew can see through the station windows
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Contrasting the beauty of the storm from above with its threat below links the detail to the novel's ideas about distance and fragility.
